newsitem.title: USA: Boeing, Lockheed to compete over new U.S. fighter.
newsitem.headline: Boeing, Lockheed to compete over new U.S. fighter.

text.p: The Pentagon on Saturday selected Lockheed Martin Corp. and Boeing Co. to compete to build 3,000 new fighter jets that could mean over $170 billion to the winner in the 21st century.
A third team headed by McDonnell Douglas Corp. was thus eliminated from the revolutionary "joint strike fighter" program in the announcement by Defense Secretary William Perry at a news conference.
The scheduled plan to narrow the competition was a major blow for St. Louis-based McDonnell, which was teamed with British Aerospace Plc and Northrop Grumman Corp. in the competition.

The radar-avoiding "stealth" jet is the biggest arms project of the early 21st century and would provide a common attack jet with variations for the U.S. Air Force, Navy and Marine Corps and the British Royal Navy.
In a hotly-contested process, Lockheed and Boeing will now build competing test models for a final selection in the year 2001. The first jets are now scheduled for delivery in 2008.
The Defense Department said it was awarding Lockheed a $718.8 million contract and Boeing got a $661.8 million contract to immediately begin work on their demonstrators.
Both firms said they were happy to go head-to-head for the lucrative prize, but CEO Harry Stonecipher of McDonnell Douglas told reporters the bitter loss was a surprise to his company.
"It's really not a good morning for us," he said.

McDonnell currently builds the Air Force F-15 fighter and the Navy-Marine F-18E/F as well as the C-17 military cargo plane. Both the F-15 and the F-18 are to be replaced by the joint strike fighter in the next century.

"Compared to current airplanes it brings a more lethal package into the theater and does it faster," said Perry, who stressed that the Pentagon learned in the 1991 Gulf War with Iraq that air dominance is now a crucial factor in battle.

Analysts say the deal could one day be worth $170 billion or more for the final winner, although some reports have speculated that it could be several times that total if spare parts and other long-term items were included.

The U.S. Air Force tentatively wants to buy 2,036 of the jets, the Marine Corps 642, the Navy 300 and the Royal Navy 60. The Marine and the British versions of the fighter would have vertical landing and takeoff ability.
Perry's announcement was a boost for Seattle-based Boeing. While the firm is the world's biggest builder of commercial jets, it has not built a figher jet since World War II.

Lockheed Martin, with big factories in Texas and California, builds the F-16 fighter and is already the nation's biggest defense contractor. It previously won the Pentagon competition to build the F-22 "stealth" fighter for the Air Force.

In addition to 3,000 joint strike fighters now planned for the four services industry executives believe another 1,000 could be sold for export to U.S. allies if future budgets can keep the massive program alive.

But some within the Pentagon have chafed at the concept of a multi-purpose design with three versions, including the "jump-jet" capability which would allow the Marines and Royal Navy to replace their current "Harrier" jets.
